Observed facts: 70‑year‑old man with known hepatic cysts, now right‑upper‑quadrant pain, early satiety, anorexia, dark urine. Initial imaging: 11.5 cm septated cyst, no bile‑duct dilatation. Labs: bilirubin 157 µmol/L (direct 111), ALP 451, AST 114, ALT 140. Aspiration cytology benign; modest biochemical improvement but cholestasis persisted. Smooth‑muscle antibody weakly positive. Liver biopsy: acute‑on‑chronic cholestatic hepatitis, mild interface change, focal bridging fibrosis, no prominent plasma‑cell infiltrate; MRCP: cyst mass effect, no duct dilatation. Recurrence with 14×12 cm cyst, possible internal haemorrhage, bilirubin 115 (direct 91), ALP 365.

Hypotheses for cholestasis: (1) Mechanical compression of intra‑hepatic ducts by the enlarging cyst despite absent radiographic dilatation; (2) Cyst‑related inflammation causing secondary cholestatic hepatitis; (3) Overlap autoimmune cholangiopathy suggested by weak smooth‑muscle antibody, though biopsy lacks plasma‑cell infiltrate; (4) Hemorrhagic cyst causing biliary obstruction or chemical cholangitis.

Limits of current data: Weak smooth‑muscle antibody is nonspecific and does not confirm autoimmune disease. Biopsy shows cholestatic pattern but cannot differentiate mechanical from immune injury; fibrosis indicates chronicity but not etiology. MRCP excludes large‑duct obstruction but cannot exclude subtle peripheral duct compression.

Proportionate next evaluation: Targeted cross‑sectional imaging with high‑resolution CT or contrast‑enhanced MRI to assess cyst‑duct relationship and vascular involvement; repeat serology for AMA, ANA, IgG4; consider ERCP or percutaneous cholangiography if ductal anatomy remains uncertain. Intervention (cyst fenestration or resection) is justified only after confirming that mechanical compression is the dominant driver; current certainty is moderate for mass effect, low for autoimmune etiology.
